title: Mrs. Mary Lucy Hamill O'Kelly Interview, 1958-05-04

blocks.x: All right, first of all, this is being recorded in Paschus Jan, April 4th, 1958. May the 4th, darling. May the 4th, 1958. Getting mixed up to start off with. All right, now, first I'd like you to tell your name, your birthplace, your date, when you lived in New Orleans, and so on, and which you... And then we'll start off on memories of jazz.

Well, this is Mrs. Mary Lucy Hamer O'Carrie. Born Mary Lucy Hamer in 1876 at Fixford, Mississippi. Lived after my marriage in 1900 at Ashwood, Louisiana, on the plantations that my husband came to New Orleans in 1909. Built a home there and lived in New Orleans until 1940. When I came to Paschus Jan to leave it. I was going home there. And I can't remember when. I first viewed jazz as being jazz. I just thought it was sort of embroidery that the niggers put on tunes that they played. They were not embedded as jazz tunes except the one I remember was the St. Louis Blues. They, these nigger bands would take any regular tune and jazz it up. They'd add little extra notes and quavers and trills and runs and syncopation and make the thing sound entirely different. For a long time we just thought it was something that they all took to naturally because I never heard any neighbor sing a tune exactly as it was written by white people. They always added some little trimming to it. They, uh, let's see, one band I remember in New Orleans was Piron's band. Played very well. There were numbers of smaller bands that played down, down we called the French Quarter and the French Quarter. Do you remember the Crossman's Day of the Rings? No, that was around 1915 I should say. And there was one very good band, I think it was after it was called the Dixie Lane Band, the Dixie Lane Band, which was, uh, downtown on the road from, let's see, from, where was it? Well, it was called the Halfway House. People who live in New Orleans would know more about the Niles because I don't remember. But I remember that our young people, teenagers, were not allowed to go to this nightclub at Halfway House, but they used to drive up near it and park and sit in the cars listening to this band. They all thought it was perfectly wonderful.
No, I don't know what band it was. It was the Halfway House. The Halfway House, and I think it, that probably was the Dixie Lane Jazz Band now, don't you think?
It's called the Halfway House Orchestra.

It's called the Halfway House Orchestra. It's called the Halfway House Orchestra. And the children thought it was wonderful. I thought it was, all this jazz was dreadful and I still do. Tell her yes. I'll ring her up later. Tell her here. And, uh, where was I? Oh, yes.
You were saying that it was horrible to me.

Well, I never cared for it. I thought it was terrible to still do. But one good thing about it, it's very, it's wonderful to dance by. Because the New Orleans bands keep such perfect time. And with the jazz, they're not wandering off in, from hither and yon to play with expression or to label on one note or to add something of their own to the expression of the piece. But they just play the notes as they come absolutely in time, never missing a beat. And that's the kind of music that people like to dance by. But it is the kind of music that I like to listen to.
Do you remember when people, did any of your contemporaries, your friends in New Orleans, like it?

I can't remember any of them that I knew. Who cared for it? Except Myra Lopum, who was a little, I was slightly shocked when she took it up so seriously. Who was that? Who was that? Myra Lopum is remember.
Oh, that was years ago. That's the last one I wanted. I mean, that's years after a lifetime. She was younger than I am.
Well, that was the first time I remembered anybody in our crowd or set of people who took jazz seriously. Who?
Who was not in your set?
Not in our set. Well, I mean, I knew her mother and father and all those people.
Well, do you remember when they started being played at debutante parties or at balls or anything like that?

Well, no. No. Dr. Sushant, Edmond Sushant had a band, the same other one, a little bit of a chap. They called it Sixth and Seventh-Eight Band. And they played jazz. They played very well. Dr. Sushant was the leader of that, the organizer of that band. And they kept it up. They used to play at different parties. And I think that's about all I know about jazz. I never cared for it, especially when I still don't.
Thank you very much, Ms. O'Kelly.
